papers.title: [Editorial] Multiple sclerosis: beyond controlling relapses
papers.summary: Few neurological diseases have seen a transformation in diagnosis and treatment as remarkable as multiple sclerosis. A chronic, heterogeneous autoimmune condition, it typically begins in early adulthood and affects over 3 million people, with women roughly three times more likely to be affected than men. Characterised by inflammation, demyelination, axonal injury, and neuronal loss, multiple sclerosis can cause relapses and gradual accumulation of disability. Three decades ago, treatment options were few and far between; today, more than 20 disease-modifying therapies are available.

papers.title: [Comment] Remibrutinib: a high-efficacy disease-modifying drug for relapsing multiple sclerosis?
papers.summary: Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitors directly modulate the functions of B lymphocytes and myeloid cells (notably macrophages and microglia) and thus target both the adaptive and innate mechanisms that contribute to the immunopathology of multiple sclerosis on either side of the blood–brain barrier. Treatment with BTK inhibitors capable of crossing the CNS could slow the progression of the disease by targeting immune cells on both sides of the blood–brain barrier.1 Although the results of clinical trials have been published for at least three BTK inhibitors (evobrutinib,2 tolebrutinib,3 and fenebrutinib4), the actual impact of this newer class of drugs on the treatment strategy for relapsing and progressive multiple sclerosis remains a subject of debate.

papers.title: [Comment] Expanding the post-EGFR TKI landscape with antibody–drug conjugates
papers.summary: Third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), increasingly combined with chemotherapy or amivantamab, are the preferred front-line treatment for EGFR-mutant non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC).1,2 With actionable resistance mechanisms often absent at progression, effective second-line therapies are needed.3 Antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs) offer one such approach, although randomised trials have yielded variable results.4–6

papers.title: [Comment] Sacituzumab tirumotecan in previously treated endometrial cancer
papers.summary: Endometrial cancer is the most common gynaecological cancer in high-income countries, the sixth most common cancer in women worldwide,1 and one of few cancers for which both the incidence and mortality rate are increasing.2,3 Although 75% of endometrial cancers present with early-stage disease when curable with surgery with or without adjuvant therapy, subsets of endometrial cancers with poor outcomes are increasing in incidence, more rapidly than cancers with better prognosis.4–6 Patients with advanced or recurrent disease are managed with platinum-based chemotherapy with or without immunotherapy, or hormonal therapy.

papers.title: [Comment] Climate–health actions: global scale-up yields economic and fiscal benefits
papers.summary: The disease burden attributable to climate change and its costs are large and growing.1 Preventing these health and economic losses in line with climate–health goals2 requires scaling up climate–health actions globally.3 Climate–health actions are policies, programmes, or other interventions in health or health-determining sectors to anticipate, prevent, prepare for, manage, or reduce health risks from climate change.4 Many climate–health actions constitute global common goods for health, safeguard human rights (eg, to health and a clean, healthy, and sustainable environment), and advance climate justice and health equity.

papers.title: [Comment] Critical condition: what are we doing about nuclear war?
papers.summary: Editorials on nuclear risk and health appeared in over 150 leading health journals in 2023 and 2025.1,2 Why, then, are we publishing this new Comment on the subject?

papers.summary: On Feb 3, 2026, The Lancet published an Expression of Concern1 for a 2006 Case Report by Gideon Koren and colleagues,2 having received new allegations of falsification of toxicological data, authorship issues, and ethical concerns. These new allegations were referred to the Research Integrity Office of The Hospital for Sick Children, Toronto, ON, Canada, for a new formal investigation. We have now received the outcome and conclusion of this investigation. The authorship issues and ethical concerns could not be fairly investigated as a meaningful participation of Gideon Koren was unlikely to be possible.

papers.title: [Comment] Offline: A manifesto for protecting public health
papers.summary: Public health institutions are being threatened by political attack. Governments that dislike being held accountable for their public health responsibilities deploy multiple means to undermine these institutions. At the European Public Health Conference, held in Bilbao, Spain, last week, Christina Pagel explained how. Contesting the science by challenging its rigour. Moving decisions from experts to political appointees. Linking funding and job security to obsequious compliance. Suppressing evidence.

papers.title: [Perspectives] Monica Geingos: advocate for adolescent health joins PMNCH
papers.summary: “Sexual and reproductive health and rights [SRHR] have been under a constant and coordinated attack”, notes Monica Geingos, former First Lady of Namibia, UNAIDS Special Ambassador for Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights, and Co-Chair of the UNAIDS Global Council on Inequality, AIDS and Pandemics. This month, Geingos brought her wide-ranging expertise to a new role as Board Chair of the Partnership for Maternal, Newborn and Child Health (PMNCH). Her leadership comes at a challenging time.

papers.title: [Perspectives] What do artists know?
papers.summary: Until the day my newborn son died, I worked as an artist. I spent each day in the studio making drawings and films, over 15 years preparing work for exhibitions, commissions, and eventually a doctorate in fine art. After he died (in my arms, peacefully, not unexpectedly), I directed everything I had learned as an artist into writing the story of his birth and death. As it turned out, over those years in the studio I had developed aptitudes well matched to drawing meaning from experience too adverse to bear.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Emerging Shamonda virus: a new threat to pregnancy?
papers.summary: The emergence of Shamonda virus in Europe raises new questions about the potential consequences of orthobunyavirus infections during pregnancy. In June, 2026, Shamonda virus was identified in cattle in central Europe, including France, Germany, and Switzerland.1 Transmission is thought to occur through bites from Culicoides midges. Detection of viral RNA in aborted bovine fetuses suggests transplacental transmission.2

papers.title: [Correspondence] Lula's new term—safeguarding science, health, and the Amazon
papers.summary: Although Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's victory in Brazil's presidential election promises executive commitment to science, public health, and environmental protection, the political reality signals a serious governability crisis. The unprecedented conservative surge in the 2026 legislative elections created a deeply hostile Congress, leaving a divided nation in which evidence-based governance, public health systems, and ecological preservation face imminent institutional gridlock. This political split, reflected in the 51·79% to 48·21% election result,1 is heightened by memories of past anti-democratic actions following the 2022 election, including civilian encampments outside military installations, demands for military intervention, and the January 2023 storming of Brasília's democratic institutions.

papers.title: [Review] Irritable bowel syndrome and related disorders of gut–brain interaction
papers.summary: Irritable bowel syndrome, chronic constipation, and functional diarrhoea are disorders of gut–brain interaction, the symptoms of which include abnormal stool consistency or frequency accompanied by varying degrees of abdominal pain, discomfort, bloating, or distension. These conditions affect 20% of the global population with a relapsing and remitting course. Risk factors include female sex, younger age, a history of common mental disorders, and acute enteric infection. The pathophysiology of irritable bowel syndrome, chronic constipation, and functional diarrhoea remain incompletely understood, but are thought to be secondary to aberrant interactions throughout the gut–brain axis, resulting in disordered gut motility and visceral hypersensitivity.

papers.title: [Editorial] Hope for efficacious vaccines for Bundibugyo virus

The outbreak is not yet under control so effective control measures are paramount. Prevention of Bundibugyo virus is currently hampered by the fact that there is no licensed vaccine for this virus but vaccine trials for Bundibugyo virus that have started recently could lead to the development of essential tools for prophylaxis.

papers.title: [Newsdesk] Research in brief
papers.summary: Current standard management of orthopaedic infections includes surgery plus ≥4 weeks of systemic antibiotic therapy. An open-label, multi-country trial investigated whether a local-antibiotic carrier implanted at the infection site during surgery could reduce the duration of systemic antibiotics. Of 475 adult participants who underwent surgery plus local antibiotic implantation, 241 received ≥4 weeks postoperative systemic antibiotics and 234 received ≤7 days postoperative systemic antibiotics. Treatment failure within 12 months occurred in 34 patients (14·1%) of 241 in the ≥4 weeks antibiotic group and in 26 patients (11·1%) of 234 in the ≤7 days antibiotic group (risk difference −3·0 percentage points [non-inferiority margin 10], 95% CI −9·0 to 3·0), highlighting that a short course of antibiotics was non-inferior to a long course.

papers.title: [Clinical Picture] Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania infantum in a Norwegian patient receiving TNF-α inhibitor therapy

He had previously received repeated courses of oral and intravenous anti-staphylococcal antibiotics for presumed facial cellulitis without improvement. Superficial cultures repeatedly grew Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus agalactiae, with persistently normal inflammatory markers.

papers.title: Genomic surveillance reveals age-structured SARS-CoV-2 transmission across settings

Transmission was strongly age-structured, with older adolescents and college-aged young adults driving early spread of new variants, while across settings staff faced comparatively little additional risk of infection.

papers.title: A natural mutation of timeless enhances mosquito thermal adaptation and malaria parasite transmission
papers.summary: Wang et al. identify a natural mutation in the mosquito circadian clock gene timeless that enhances male mating performance at high temperatures and malaria parasite susceptibility in females. The tim mutation stabilizes per expression under high temperatures, promoting AKH-dependent energy mobilization and FAR-dependent pheromone production in males, whereas impaired antiparasitic immunity promotes infection in females, revealing how clock-gene variation can shape both mosquito thermal adaptation and malaria parasite transmission.

papers.title: RNA folding drives species-dependent host mRNA partitioning in Ebola virus condensates
papers.summary: Viral condensates are increasingly recognized as hubs for viral replication, but how they interact with host RNAs is poorly understood. This study reveals that Ebola virus condensates selectively recruit and stabilize host mRNAs, reshaping antiviral gene expression in ways that differ between humans and bats.

papers.title: Myelin pathology is a key feature of X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism
papers.summary: A humanized mouse model of X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism reveals widespread loss of myelin-forming oligodendrocytes, a pathology also seen in patient brains that points to a contributor to this movement disorder.

papers.title: CD19 CAR T cell therapy alters disease-associated immune signatures in multiple sclerosis
papers.summary: In a preliminary case series of five individuals with multiple sclerosis, CD19 CAR T cell therapy is associated with the expansion of CAR T cells in the CSF and sustained reductions in CSF disease biomarkers, providing preliminary evidence for compartment-specific immunomodulation beyond peripheral B cell depletion.

papers.title: Genome writing reveals SVA retrotransposon consequences in X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism
papers.summary: Genomic conditional humanization of the mouse Taf1 locus with an XDP patient-derived allele recapitulates key molecular and neuropathological features of XDP, revealing that intronic SVA transcription impairs TAF1 expression and drives striatal degeneration. CRISPRa-mediated Taf1 activation suggests a potential therapeutic strategy.

papers.title: Paleogenomics illuminates mobility and changing lifeways in Chalcolithic Anatolia
papers.summary: Contrary to the stark decline in the archaeological records in Chalcolithic Anatolia (c. 6000–3000 BCE), paleogenomics reveals that populations grew and/or became more mobile, suggesting changing lifeways. Genetic admixture with populations from eastern regions continued throughout this period, and early evidence of movement between Anatolia and the Eurasian Steppe appeared.

papers.title: Evolutionary repurposing of a pore-forming toxin drives epithelial remodeling during terrestrial adaptation
papers.summary: In African lungfish, an evolutionarily repurposed pore-forming toxin, Protop-CrTX-A, switches its source of secretion from goblet cells to infiltrating granulocytes during estivation, driving epithelial remodeling associated with adaptation to terrestrial life.

papers.title: Sub-second dopamine reinforcement shapes juvenile social play
papers.summary: Dopamine acts moment by moment to reinforce the specific actions that make up juvenile social play. Disrupted reinforcement underlies social deficits in a Shank3-deficient autism model, and correcting it in real time restores normal play.

papers.title: The blood-brain barrier imports diverse neuroprotective proteins through pathways impaired early in Alzheimer’s disease models
papers.summary: Bioorthogonal proteomics reveals that the blood-brain barrier (BBB) imports diverse plasma proteins to specific brain cell types through receptor-mediated transport, a process dysregulated early in an Alzheimer’s model. Restoring one diminished protein, liver-derived apolipoprotein A1, rescues Alzheimer’s glial and neuronal dysfunction, recasting the BBB as an interface recruiting peripheral signals for brain health.

papers.title: COP1 is a temperature-responsive switch in Arabidopsis
papers.summary: COP1, a central integrator of light signaling, senses temperature via an intrinsically disordered region, suggesting how thermomorphogenesis can be modulated according to different climates.

papers.title: Nicotianamine-driven nickel transport to sink organs underpins maize productivity
papers.summary: A node-phloem-localized nicotianamine efflux transporter in maize regulates Ni delivery to sink organs, including seeds, where Ni-dependent urease activity promotes amino acid metabolism, revealing an unappreciated role of Ni in the yield formation of graminaceous plants.

papers.title: Reconstructing developmental and disease progression with sample-level embeddings
papers.summary: An scRNA-seq framework that embeds each sample by the density distribution of its cells across cellular states is used to resolve continuous variation in infection, neurodegeneration, embryonic development, and whole-organism perturbation that discrete sample labels obscure.

papers.title: CRISPR mutagenesis of the MYC locus reveals a druggable ultraconserved RNA element
papers.summary: CRISPR tiling mutagenesis of the 10-kb human MYC locus mapped the fitness landscape of an entire human gene at base-pair resolution. This unbiased interrogation revealed that 67% of functionally essential base pairs are noncoding. An ultraconserved RNA regulatory element was identified that controls MYC localization and can be therapeutically targeted to suppress cancer cell growth in patient-derived tumor organoids.

papers.title: Industrialization drives convergent microbiome and host physiological shifts in the human metaorganism
papers.summary: Integration of microbiome omics and host data from globally diverse human populations shows that industrialization restructures gut microbial ecosystems and intestinal physiology. These shifts include reduced microbial diversity, compositional heterogeneity, and community stability; altered intestinal immune and physiological responses; and limited cross-population portability of microbiome-based disease predictors.

papers.title: Convergent genomic evolution of human gut bacteria along an industrialization gradient
papers.summary: Analysis of globally diverse gut bacterial isolate genomes shows that host environments across the industrialization gradient shape genome remodeling and convergent selection, while industrialization is linked to increased HGT-driven gene acquisition and expanded genome size.

papers.title: TECR palmitoylation triggers a necrotic cell death program driving acute liver injury
papers.summary: We identify a TECR palmitoylation-dependent necrotic cell death (TPNCD) pathway. Blocking TPNCD genetically or pharmacologically protects against immune- and drug-induced liver injury, revealing a therapeutic strategy for hepatic injury.

papers.title: Subsistence transition preceded population turnover in the eastern Colombian Andes
papers.summary: Ancient DNA data and stable isotope data from the eastern Colombian Andes reveal that C4-enriched resources were incorporated into local food webs during five millennia of genetic continuity and that a later population turnover introduced people with ancestry admixed between that found in Chibchan-related groups and that found at the Amazonian-Andean interface.

papers.title: Fatty acid desaturation controls cellular fate decisions between senescence and ferroptosis
papers.summary: Polyunsaturated fatty acid metabolism shapes cell fate decisions: loss of DGLA favors senescence, whereas DGLA repletion triggers ferroptosis.

papers.title: Age-dependent structural evolution of a functional amyloid contributes to memory impairment in Drosophila
papers.summary: In the aging Drosophila brain, Orb2 amyloids required for long-term memory undergo structural remodeling, shifting from translation-promoting assemblies to destabilization-resistant, translation-deficient states. Rebalancing Orb2 toward youthful, translationally active assemblies improves memory in old flies.

papers.title: Genetic coupling of floral rewards and signals underlies pollinator attraction
papers.summary: Floral rewards and signals must be coordinated to attract pollinators, but the underlying genetic mechanisms remain poorly understood. Using melon as a model system, this study reveals how the developmental regulator YAB5 coordinates nectar production, flower opening, and floral signals to promote bee visitation.

papers.title: Innate sensor responses set a supra-unitary threshold for viral replication
papers.summary: Single-cell analysis reveals that viral replication requires a supra-unitary input of viral genomes, which varies with different viruses and cell types. We show that supra-unitary viral genome quantities, independently of viral protein synthesis, activate negative feedback regulators of RIG-I, MDA-5, and PKR, suppressing the innate immune response and allowing replication.

papers.title: Long-range actin-driven endosymbiont mobility in an animal-algal symbiosis
papers.summary: Hundreds to thousands of dinoflagellate symbionts (Amphidinium sp., 10–20 μm in size) move up to hundreds of micrometers inside the tissue of their acoel worm hosts (Waminoa sp., millimeters in size). Host actin machinery is primarily responsible for driving symbiont mobility at speeds around 1 μm/s, and symbionts move inside ribbon-like host cells (∼200 nm thin), which stretch to accommodate symbionts moving through them.

papers.title: Somatic DNA-repeat expansions initiate distinct yet analogous changes in Huntington’s disease cortical and striatal neurons
papers.summary: Single-cell-resolution analysis of brain tissue in Huntington's disease (HD) reveals that cortical and striatal neurons pass through analogous biological changes, each initiated by a neuron's own expanding DNA repeat. In cortical neurons, as in striatal neurons, the DNA repeat expands somatically over decades (phases A and B) and becomes toxic at about 150 CAGs, initiating cell-identity erosion (phase C), the formation of nuclear inclusions of aggregated HTT protein, a derepression crisis (phase D), and then death of the neuron.

papers.title: Multimodal spatial transcriptomics redefines cortical pathology in Huntington’s disease
papers.summary: By using multimodal spatial transcriptomics to measure somatic repeat expansion, huntingtin pathology, and transcriptional profile in every cell of intact tissue sections, we identify in the Huntington’s disease cortex that large somatic CAG repeat expansions are linked to the selective loss of L5–6 NP and L6b deep-layer excitatory neurons. Intranuclear inclusions of huntingtin were most prevalent at intermediate somatic repeat expansions and were associated with broader transcriptional changes than somatic repeat expansion alone.

papers.title: In vivo genome-editing therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy: Preclinical studies and first-in-human trial
papers.summary: A single-dose AAV-CRISPR therapy restores dystrophin in humanized DMD mice and achieves durable editing with manageable safety in non-human primates. In a first-in-human DMD trial, the therapy yields molecular evidence of muscle editing but reveals a fatal dose-dependent immune complication, highlighting the urgent need to expand the safety margin of systemic AAV-CRISPR treatments.

papers.title: Perforin triggers iron-induced mitochondrial damage to drive ferroptosis and anti-tumor immunity
papers.summary: Perforin is best known for delivering granzymes into tumor cells, but this study shows it has a second, independent killing function: it drives iron uptake and mitochondrial iron overload that trigger ferroptosis. This granzyme-independent pathway links cytotoxic immunity to iron metabolism, predicts patient response to checkpoint blockade, and points to iron supplementation as a possible lever for boosting anti-tumor immunity.

papers.title: Taurine lowers inflammaging by regulating the NLRP3 inflammasome in macrophages
papers.summary: Taurine levels increase with age in mice and humans. Boosting taurine levels even further in aged mice increases health span and dampens inflammation through its regulation of the NLRP3 inflammasome.

papers.title: Cell-state-specific metabolic networks govern ferroptosis versus apoptosis in small cell lung cancer
papers.summary: SCLC cell states dictate how cancer cells respond to metabolic stress, revealing how metabolic plasticity determines whether the cells undergo ferroptosis or apoptosis.

papers.title: Intracellular defenses and receptor masking both limit the success of a clinical Pseudomonas aeruginosa phage family
papers.summary: Yee et al. reveal that clinical P. aeruginosa blocks a group of clinically used phages, Pbunavirus phages, at two levels: by masking the conserved core-LPS receptor and deploying intracellular defenses. They show that tail-fiber and anti-defense engineering, with predictable resistance trade-offs, could be exploited therapeutically.

papers.title: Population-scale identification of gut commensals that antagonize antibiotic-resistant pathogens
papers.summary: Zhang et al. identify gut commensals inversely associated with pathogenic taxa linked to antibiotic resistance genes across global populations. By integrating metagenomics, peptide discovery, and experimental validation, they highlight F. prausnitzii and its candidate antimicrobial peptides as potential microbiome-derived strategies for reducing the gut antibiotic resistance burden.

papers.title: Degradation of mucin O-glycans by a human gut symbiont requires a complex enzyme repertoire and promotes colonization
papers.summary: Schaus et al. reveal how the gut symbiont Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron uses a coordinated repertoire of enzymes to degrade colonic mucin O-glycans. Enzymes that act on terminal O-glycan decorations are important for colonization, identifying key steps that may shape host-microbiota interactions at the intestinal mucus barrier.

papers.title: Microbial metabolism of methotrexate produces a STAT3 signaling molecule that alleviates gut inflammation
papers.summary: Cho et al. show that gut microbial metabolism of methotrexate generates DAMPA. DAMPA promotes mitochondrial function and protects against intestinal inflammation, revealing how microbial drug metabolism can generate beneficial signals that influence host physiology.

papers.title: Microbial products trigger chemosensory dialogues through intestinal G protein-coupled receptors
papers.summary: Kadoki et al. developed GPCR-seq, a high-throughput platform to identify how the gut senses environmental chemicals. They discovered gut microbial products that activate intestinal receptors, triggering serotonin release or linking to inflammatory bowel disease. This work provides a scalable template for decoding how host-microbe communication influences human health.

papers.title: Secretory bile salt hydrolases regulate niche displacement and gut colonization of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus
papers.summary: Hasegawa et al. show that a class of bile salt hydrolases (BSHs) harbored by Bacteroidales species promote elimination of vancomycin-resistant enterococcus (VRE) in the presence of Lachnospiraceae bai+ bacteria. In the gut, bacteria producing this subclass of BSH eliminate and displace VRE through deoxycholic acid (DCA) production.

papers.title: The transcription factor TOX maintains stemness circuits that sustain longevity and multipotency of progenitor CD4+ T cells in chronic infection
papers.summary: Understanding the molecular circuitry controlling CD4+ TEX cell differentiation may provide opportunities to harness CD4+ T cell help and promote clearance of chronic viral infections and tumors. Lundh et al. find that TOX configures the transcriptional and epigenetic landscape of CD4+ Tpex cells, thus enabling differentiation and survival of CD4+ TEX cell responses.

papers.title: Brain border-associated macrophages rhythmically scavenge amyloid-beta and regulate vascular amyloid pathology
papers.summary: Circadian disruption is a major risk factor for neurodegenerative disease. Barr et al. find that brain border-associated macrophages (BAMs) are clock-entrained and more effectively scavenge fluid-borne substrates, including amyloid-beta, during rest. Circadian disruption of BAMs precipitates perivascular and leptomeningeal amyloid pathology, linking rhythms in brain border immunity to the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative disease.

papers.title: Human interferon-α autoantibody development broadens reactivity and enables functional synergy
papers.summary: Human autoantibodies against IFN-α predispose to severe viral disease, yet their origins remain poorly understood. Groen et al. trace development of plasma autoreactivity against IFN-α subtypes, revealing how initially narrow specificity evolves into broad and potent neutralization. Structural and functional analyses uncover distinct modes of IFN-α recognition and show that epitope-specific antibodies co-operate to enhance neutralization and activate Fc-effector function.

papers.title: Granzyme K is a driver of age-related tissue remodeling and functional decline independently of age-associated immune dysfunction
papers.summary: T cell-derived Granzyme K (GzmK) increases with age, but its contribution to immune and organismal aging remains unclear. Kannangara et al. demonstrate that GzmK drives age-related tissue fibrosis and organ dysfunction without contributing to immune aging, revealing that these processes can be uncoupled and identifying GzmK as a potential therapeutic target for promoting healthy aging without compromising immune function.

papers.title: Tumor-to-dendritic cell reprogramming induces immunogenic lymphoid structures across cancers
papers.summary: Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) support effective cancer immunity but remain difficult to induce experimentally. Ascic, Chatelain, et al. establish tumor-to-cDC1 reprogramming as a strategy to generate immunogenic TLSs across multiple cancers, uncovering how localized migratory cDC1 and CD40-dependent T cell interactions coordinate local and systemic cellular and humoral immunity.

papers.title: A microbiome-reactive TMIGD2hi Th17 subset is spatially enriched at the intestinal epithelium and expanded in inflammatory bowel disease
papers.summary: Our understanding of how commensal-specific CD4+ T cells respond to intestinal inflammation is limited. Pedersen et al. define the phenotypic diversity of human CD4+ T cells recognizing a defined Bacteroidales epitope across disease settings. This revealed a TMIGD2hi Th17 phenotype that expands in inflamed tissue. More broadly, this work underscores the malleability of microbiota-specific T cells during inflammatory bowel disease.

papers.title: Human brain cellular xenografts in neuroimmunology and beyond
papers.summary: Human brain cellular xenograft (HBCX) models are emerging as a system to study human brain physiology and pathology in vivo. Mancuso and colleagues discuss how HBCXs enable in vivo interrogation of human-specific brain cell biology, neuroimmunology, disease modeling, and genetic risk and their potential for functional genomics, therapeutic discovery, and preclinical assessment of cell-based therapies for central nervous system disorders.

papers.title: NF-κB phosphorylation controls enhancer selection to shape the inflammatory gene program
papers.summary: Activation of the NF-κB pathway triggers diverse inflammatory outcomes despite similar upstream signaling. Leão et al. show that Ser276 phosphorylation of the p65 subunit of NF-κB p65 promotes CBP/p300 recruitment, enabling latent enhancer engagement and activation, and revealing an enhancer-selection mechanism that controls a distinct gene expression program shaping inflammatory and antimicrobial immune responses.

papers.title: WHO Reports Highest Number of Cholera Deaths in Decades
papers.summary: The World Health Organization (WHO) found that deaths from cholera increased in 2025, despite a lower number of reported cases. The WHO also provided updated data on bacterial meningitis in Africa in 2025 as well as human plague.

papers.title: Global Heart Failure Burden Increased Between 1990 and 2023
papers.summary: The global burden of heart failure increased sharply from 1990 to 2023, reaching an estimated 56 million cases worldwide, according to a cross-sectional study published in JAMA Cardiology.

papers.summary: The American College of Cardiology (ACC) released new guidance on blood pressure management for patients with resistant hypertension.

papers.title: Steatotic Liver Disease: A Global Problem
papers.summary: This Medical News article discusses international efforts to determine the prevalence and increase awareness and detection of steatotic liver disease, which affects an estimated 1.7 billion people worldwide, including most individuals with obesity or type 2 diabetes.

papers.title: The Rise in Testosterone Therapy for Women
papers.summary: This Medical News article discusses growing use of testosterone therapy among women, and a US Food and Drug Administration public workshop that explored the current evidence on its use beyond sexual function.

papers.title: Obesity and Starvation
papers.summary: The essence of the successful method for reducing weight … lies in keeping the intake of energy below that of the output. Theoretically, complete fasting constitutes the most prompt method of accomplishing the end sought. It is a well-recognized fact, however, that starvation prolonged over a period of more than a few days, either voluntarily or as an incident of disease, may lead to unpleasant symptoms. Headache, nausea and dizziness portend the existence of conditions that are not exactly normal, and frequently they can be made to disappear promptly by the ingestion of even a little food. Most modern “treatments” for obesity, therefore, consist in underfeeding rather than complete fasting, particular care being directed to conserving the protein of the body so that the reduction in weight shall represent essentially a loss of body fat oxidized to furnish energy to the underfed individual.

papers.title: Compounded GLP-1 Dispensing Patterns and Vitamin B 12  Coformulation
papers.summary: This study uses comprehensive prescription drug monitoring program data to describe compounded weight-loss prescriptions, rates of self-payment, out-of-state dispensing, and the ingredients contained in compounded GLP-1s.

papers.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines on Antiviral Therapies for Adults With COVID-19 Infection
papers.summary: To the Editor The JAMA Clinical Guidelines Synopsis by Dr Leung and colleagues offered a useful risk-stratified overview of antiviral therapy for mild to moderate COVID-19 infection. Two descriptions of drug precautions may nonetheless benefit from clarification because both concern prescribing safety.

papers.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines on Antiviral Therapies for Adults With COVID-19 Infection—Reply
papers.summary: In Reply We thank Dr Tseng and colleagues for identifying 2 areas of our JAMA Clinical Guidelines Synopsis that warrant clarification. We agree with both points.

papers.summary: The history and future of breast cancer research and treatment are discussed by JAMA Senior Editor Derek C. Angus, MD, MPH, and Nancy E. Davidson, MD, chief academic officer and executive vice president of the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, for this episode of the Healthy Dialogue podcast.

papers.title: Prone Positioning for Infants With Bronchiolitis and HFNC Support
papers.summary: To the Editor The PROPOSITIS trial was a large study evaluating prone positioning in infants with bronchiolitis receiving high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) support. Although the primary outcome was not statistically significant, the observed effect size suggests that further investigation remains warranted.

papers.title: Prone Positioning for Infants With Bronchiolitis and HFNC Support—Reply
papers.summary: In Reply We thank Drs van Egmond and Mulier for their letter about the PROPOSITIS study. They raise an important point regarding the need to report the prone positioning procedure and the effects of prone positioning beyond transpulmonary pressure gradients.

papers.title: Patient Information: Childhood Obesity
papers.summary: This JAMA Patient Page describes how childhood obesity is defined, how common it is, and the risk factors and health conditions associated with childhood obesity.

papers.title: Social History
papers.summary: Your emergence was always in light blue cotton nightclothes, shuffling already stooped to pick up the paper. You did your primary survey right side, above the fold but no news was good enough; you salvaged the Travel section and threw the rest away, and so it was since your wife died or your hair greyed— I knew no more of your story than this morning ritual, than that you wasted money on a newspaper subscription when you should have bought a Lonely Planet guide.

papers.title: “He Lives Alone”: The Social History and Detachment in Poetry and Medicine
papers.summary: The poem “Social History” considers how we distance ourselves from others. Although critiques of medical care frequently bemoan unfeeling clinical detachment, here distancing begins outside of the hospital in the very act of observing and then in the writing of the poem itself. The speaker blithely describes a man through the morning ritual she watches: he emerges from his home in “light/blue cotton nightclothes,” retrieves the newspaper, saves the Travel section, discards the rest. This knowledge is intimate yet incomplete, neighborly yet espied, even slightly invasive. The poem, then, implicates itself as almost a failed “social history,” describing a life observed but not understood. papers.title: Obesity in Children Aged 2 to 12 Years
papers.summary: This narrative review examines obesity in children aged 2 to 12 years, including its epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnosis, and treatment, such as intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment and approved pharmacotherapies.

papers.title: Illicit Injectable Peptides
papers.summary: To the Editor Dr Piatkowski and colleagues described how unapproved injectable peptides are promoted for muscle growth, recovery, and antiaging, despite limited human evidence. The same phenomenon is already emerging in Brazil, demonstrating how rapidly digital markets can carry unsupported health claims across national borders.

papers.title: Illicit Injectable Peptides—Reply
papers.summary: In Reply We thank Dr Janovsky for highlighting the emergence of illicit peptide markets in Brazil and for extending the discussion beyond the jurisdictions considered in our original Viewpoint. Janovsky’s observations reinforce our central argument that the rapid expansion of unapproved peptide use is no longer a country-specific regulatory issue, but an increasingly global public health challenge. The Brazilian experience is striking because it mirrors patterns emerging elsewhere. Illicit peptides are increasingly marketed online using remarkably consistent narratives centered on recovery, muscle growth, healthy aging, and health optimization, despite limited human evidence supporting these claims. As Janovsky notes, concerns extend beyond efficacy to product quality, manufacturing standards, and unsupported therapeutic claims.

papers.title: Nicotinamide Riboside for Patients With Early-Stage Parkinson Disease
papers.summary: This randomized trial assesses the effect of oral nicotinamide riboside treatment for 52 weeks vs placebo on clinical outcomes among patients with early Parkinson disease.

papers.title: Nicotinamide Riboside for Patients With Early-Stage Parkinson Disease Research Summary
papers.summary: This trial evaluated whether oral nicotinamide riboside improves clinical outcomes in patients with early Parkinson disease.

papers.title: Trials of Treatment Deescalation, Deimplementation, and Discontinuation
papers.summary: To the Editor As therapeutic options expand and polypharmacy and drug-related harms become increasingly common, evidence-based treatment discontinuation is becoming an important clinical priority. Dr Huang and colleagues’ timely overview of deescalation and discontinuation trials raised a fundamental methodological question: what exactly do these trials estimate?

papers.title: Trials of Treatment Deescalation, Deimplementation, and Discontinuation—Reply
papers.summary: In Reply Drs Mathioudakis and Chatzimavridou-Grigoriadou raise an excellent point in response to our JAMA+ Trials themed Editorial on deescalation, discontinuation, and deimplementation trials: often, the effects of discontinuing a health intervention extend beyond the simple absence of benefit (or harm) from continued intervention use. Instead, the act or process of discontinuation itself can have direct, important, and potentially time-dependent effects on outcomes—for example, through withdrawal or rebound effects that can manifest after intervention discontinuation and may or may not subside over time.

papers.title: Medicare and Bureau of Health Workforce and Funded Primary Care Residency Positions
papers.summary: To the Editor We are writing about the Research Letter “Changes in Specialty and Geography of Medicare’s New Residency Positions,” which reported that Medicare-funded expansion has not substantially increased primary care or rural training capacity. However, we would like to highlight an important limitation of specialty-based workforce estimates: residency positions labeled as primary care may not accurately reflect the production of physicians who enter primary care practice. Because these estimates rely on specialty designation, they may overstate primary care workforce contributions and fail to capture graduates’ postresidency practice.

papers.title: Medicare and Bureau of Health Workforce and Funded Primary Care Residency Positions—Reply
papers.summary: In Reply We appreciate the comments by Drs Hayes and Dapkins regarding our study on Medicare-funded GME positions and the relevancy of the THCGME program to the US physician workforce policy landscape.

papers.title: Postpartum Initiation of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists Among Commercially Insured Women in the US
papers.summary: This cross-sectional study examines glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist initiation rates among postpartum women with commercial insurance in the US.

papers.title: Equitable Access to GLP-1 Receptor Agonists—Essential but Not Accessible
papers.summary: This Perspective discusses the actions needed to improve accessibility of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, especially in low- and middle-income countries, after their addition to the World Health Organization’s (WHO) Model List of Essential Medicines.

papers.title: Multimodal Care for Obesity in the GLP-1 Therapy Era
papers.summary: This Perspective urges multimodal management of obesity that extends beyond pharmacological treatment to screening, early management, and intensive behavioral therapy across the life course.

papers.title: Risk Stratification in Lean MASLD
papers.summary: Evaluation of metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) relies on the “visible proxy” of body size. This is understandable: excess adiposity, associated with insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and cardiometabolic dysfunction, is a major driver of the global MASLD epidemic. Yet this framing becomes misleading when body mass index (BMI) is treated as a surrogate for metabolic risk. A clinically important minority of patients develop MASLD despite a BMI in the normal range. These patients, commonly described as having lean MASLD, reveal the limitations of an obesity-centered clinical approach and ultimately challenge the assumption that normal body weight implies low liver-related risk.

papers.title: Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillators for Patients With an LVEF >35%
papers.summary: The implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) remains a cornerstone therapy for the prevention of sudden cardiac death. Randomized clinical trials have demonstrated a survival benefit with ICDs for primary prevention in patients with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 35% or less; therefore, professional guideline recommendations on ICDs are based on this LVEF cutoff. However, most individuals who experience a sudden cardiac arrest do not have significant left ventricular dysfunction. Admittedly, these LVEF cutoffs are arbitrary, and the risk of sudden cardiac death is not dichotomous.

papers.summary: Autoimmune disease is on the rise, and while no direct connection has been made, evidence suggests environmental toxins such as nanoplastics may be contributing to the increased incidence. A key factor in the onset of autoimmunity is inflammation; yet how nanoplastics impact innate immune function is unclear. Here, we exposed primary human neutrophils, macrophages, and endothelial cells to biocorona-coated polystyrene nanoplastics at physiologically relevant concentrations. papers.title: Continuous generation of short-lived resident effector CD8 T cells sustains alopecia areata
papers.summary: CD8 T cells mediating chronic tissue inflammation have been thought to depend on stem-like progenitors that self-renew and replenish cytotoxic effector cells or exhausted progeny. papers.summary: Early life offers a window to establish lasting tolerance to dietary and commensal microbial antigens. How developing gut lymph nodes balance tolerance and immunity remains unclear. papers.title: FOLR2 Identifies Functionally Distinct Decidual Macrophage Populations that Coordinate Immune and Tissue Remodelling During Human Labour
papers.summary: The initiation of human labour remains incompletely understood, although mounting evidence implicates decidual macrophages in this process. Despite this, macrophage heterogeneity remains poorly defined, with current macrophage classification systems, including M1/M2, failing to capture their biological diversity. Here, we investigate whether macrophage differentiation state, defined by expression of the tissue residency marker FOLR2, provides a more informative framework for characterising human decidual macrophages at term. RNA sequencing and flow cytometry identified FOLR2- and FOLR2+ macrophages as transcriptionally and phenotypically distinct populations. papers.title: A Dysregulated Peripheral Immune Landscape Favors the Expansion of Epstein-Barr Virus positive Age-Associated B Cells in Multiple Sclerosis
papers.summary: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a major risk factor for multiple sclerosis (MS), but the underlying mechanisms are not yet known. Here, we use single-cell RNA sequencing coupled with targeted EBV transcript enrichment to characterize host immune and viral transcriptional dynamics following EBV ex vivo infection of PBMCs from people with active MS compared to healthy controls (HC). Early responses to EBV were dominated by differences in monocyte and NK cells, including EBV transcripts in monocytes prior to ex vivo infection. At later time points, expansion of EBV-infected age-associated B-cells (ABCs) and increased expression of T-cell exhaustion- associated markers were elevated in MS. papers.title: Three-Dimensional Refractive Index Patterns Distinguish CD57-Defined Subsets of Human Memory T Cells
papers.summary: Distinguishing T-cell subsets is important for characterizing immune differentiation, but label-free classification is challenging because closely related subsets have overlapping biophysical properties. We combined holotomography with a three-dimensional convolutional neural network to classify primary human T cells from their refractive index (RI) tomograms. Fluorescence-activated cell sorting defined four reference populations: CD4+, naive CD8+, and CD57- and CD57+ memory CD8+ T cells. Dedicated binary classifiers achieved 97.70% accuracy for naive versus CCR7- memory CD8+ cells and 94.44% for CD57- versus CD57+ memory CD8+ cells. Although the memory subsets overlapped in whole-cell descriptors, their volumetric RI patterns supported classification. These findings establish a basis for investigating intrinsic optical phenotypes associated with CD57-defined T-cell differentiation.

papers.title: Biphasic glycocalyx remodelling balances immune cell recruitment and tissue damage during influenza infection
papers.summary: The endothelial glycocalyx is a glycan-rich barrier lining blood vessels that regulates immune cell recruitment, whose role in viral infection is unknown. Using a murine influenza model, we reveal that the lung endothelial glycocalyx undergoes coordinated biphasic remodelling: early shedding followed by substantial accumulation during peak immune activation. Genetic deletion of heparanase, the enzyme driving early glycocalyx shedding, reduced immune cell lung infiltration and improved host recovery. Together, these findings reveal that coordinated endothelial and immune cell glycocalyx remodelling is an active and previously unrecognised regulator of the balance between antiviral immune cell recruitment and tissue protection.

papers.title: The decidual microenvironment shapes neutrophil subsets that promote extravillous trophoblast invasion in early pregnancy
papers.summary: Successful establishment of the maternal-fetal interface is a critical process during early pregnancy, ensuring healthy fetal development. A critical phase in establishing the utero-placental blood supply is the invasion of extravillous trophoblasts (EVTs) into the maternal spiral arteries, marking the transformation of the endometrium into the decidua. By separating the EVT invaded decidua (iDec) and EVT non-invaded decidua (niDec), we demonstrate that neutrophils dominate the iDec immune landscape during early human pregnancy. papers.title: Spatially-Organized Adaptive Immune Niches in Granulomas Dictate Local Defense and Correlate with Disease Severity in Tuberculosis Patients
papers.summary: The cellular composition and spatial organization of immune responses within tuberculosis (TB) granulomas have been increasingly characterized, yet how these spatially organized immune cell populations coordinate local adaptive immunity remains largely unknown. Here, we integrated single-cell multi-omics, spatial transcriptomics, and immune receptor profiling to construct a comprehensive spatial atlas of human TB granulomas. We identified two concentric adaptive immune niches surrounding the central necrotic core. The outer niche comprised granuloma-associated tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) that supported TFH-B cell interactions and exhibited functional germinal center-like features associated with antigen-driven B-cell maturation toward FCRL5 antibody-producing cells. papers.title: Proteome-wide antibody responses to PfSPZ Vaccine include cross-reactive antibodies that correlate with protection from malaria
papers.summary: The PfSPZ Vaccine induces both humoral and cellular immunity. While T cells are likely critical for protection, previous analyses of antibody correlates have focused on select antigens. Here, we apply a proteome-wide approach to examine antibody responses across the entire Plasmodium falciparum (Pf) proteome. Sera from malaria-naive volunteers immunized with high doses of PfSPZ Vaccine were probed using whole proteome Pf protein microarrays and high-density Pf peptide microarrays. Both platforms identified antibody responses that significantly correlated with protection, including responses to the immunodominant Pf circumsporozoite protein (CSP). papers.title: Evaluation of urine lipoarabinomannan and host response signatures for culture-negative tuberculosis using composite criteria and Bayesian Latent Class Analysis
papers.summary: Abstract Background: Culture-negative TB is a major diagnostic challenge, and the lack of a reliable reference standard hinders evaluation of non-sputum diagnostic tests. We compared composite reference criteria and Bayesian latent class analysis to examine how different culture-negative TB definitions affect disease classification and evaluations of two non-sputum biomarkers: urine lipoarabinomannan (uLAM) and host transcriptional response signatures (HRS). Methods: Urine and blood samples from 112 sputum culture-negative and 55 culture-positive symptomatic adults evaluated for tuberculosis from South Africa, Uganda, and Kenya, alongside 17 controls with other respiratory conditions, were analyzed using uLAM and HRS assays. papers.title: Nonstructural Protein 1 (NS1)-based IgG FcγR competition Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assays (ELISAs) for highly specific serological profiling of previous flavivirus exposures
papers.summary: Background: Due to extensive antibody cross-reactivity, serological discrimination of IgG antibodies elicited by exposure to different flaviviruses remains challenging. We aimed to develop and validate highly discriminative IgG ELISAs employing an Fc{gamma} receptor (Fc{gamma}R) capture platform and recombinant competitor molecules to suppress cross-reactive responses. Methods: IgG ELISAs targeting Dengue virus (DENV), Zika virus (ZIKV), and West Nile virus (WNV) were established using immobilized human Fc{gamma}RIIA for antibody capture and soluble, labeled nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) as antigen. papers.title: Long-term transmission chains fueling the drug-resistant tuberculosis burden in Southern Brazil
papers.summary: Background Tuberculosis (TB) remains a leading infectious cause of death, with drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) challenging disease control. Brazil has a high TB burden, and Rio Grande do Sul state reports persistently high incidence and drug-resistance rates. The drivers shaping the regional DR-TB burden remain poorly characterised. Methods We conducted genomic surveillance of confirmed DR-TB cases in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, from January 2023 to September 2024. Clinical isolates underwent genotypic (gDST) and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (pDST) and whole-genome sequencing (WGS). We analyzed 33 newly sequenced genomes and 267 historical Mycobacterium tuberculosis genomes collected in 2011-2019 to characterize resistance, transmission, and spatiotemporal patterns and estimate the contributions of transmitted and acquired rifampicin resistance. papers.title: Upper respiratory microbiome and host immune signatures associated with SARS-CoV-2 susceptibility and illness in a human challenge model
papers.summary: The upper respiratory tract (URT) microbiome modulates the local mucosal immune environment, with potential implications for respiratory viral infection susceptibility and outcomes. We leveraged a first-in-human SARS-CoV-2 challenge study in 34 healthy young adults, 18 of whom became infected, to characterize host gene expression and microbiome composition and dynamics in nasal and throat samples collected before viral inoculation and over the subsequent 14 days. Compared with participants who remained uninfected, participants who became infected had elevated baseline nasal expression of gene modules related to interferon, innate inflammatory, and neutrophil responses, as well as a delayed transcriptional response to viral challenge. papers.title: The effect of smallpox vaccination: unique insights gained from Danish post-honeymoon epidemics 200 years ago
papers.summary: BackgroundHistorically, the Variola virus caused deadly smallpox epidemics in children. In Copenhagen, transmission was halted by 1810 when [~]90% of children were vaccinated following the introduction of a mandatory single-dose vaccine program. A 14-year honeymoon period followed, but in 1824 smallpox re-emerged as a milder disease of adults. papers.summary: BackgroundSwab-based molecular testing for tuberculosis (TB) could provide a near point-of-care (nPOC) diagnostic for children. papers.summary: Soil-transmitted helminth control relies on mass anthelmintic treatment, yet helminth-anthelmintic-microbiome interactions and their role on treatment response remain poorly understood. papers.summary: Urinary tract infections are commonly caused by bacteria whose antibiotic susceptibility varies between clinical settings.1 We studied urinary isolates from 95 patients with suspected infection at Lahore General Hospital, Pakistan, between July and December 2023. papers.title: Improving respiratory virus forecasts by capturing the effects of school holidays, public holidays and seasonal changes in transmission
papers.summary: Respiratory viruses impose a substantial burden of morbidity and mortality globally, and models that forecast this burden are widely used to support public health decision-making. papers.summary: IntroductionThis is an immunohistochemical (IHC) pilot study of adult patients who underwent allogeneic stem cell transplantation (alloSCT) for hematological disease and had BKPyV reactivation (BKPyV viruria) as well as graft-versus-host-disease (GvHD) to investigate, if there is an association between these two diseases. papers.summary: RationalePoint-of-care lung ultrasound is portable and radiation-free and could extend tuberculosis screening to settings without chest radiography, but no standardized criteria exist for interpreting it for tuberculosis. papers.title: A rapid and sensitive Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) assay for detection of mecA antibiotic resistance gene in clinical and food bacterial isolates
papers.summary: An advanced LAMP assay targeting the mecA gene in methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) was developed and validated using clinical and foodborne S. aureus isolates. papers.title: Practical evaluation of AI models to forecast a respiratory seasonal epidemic in Canada
papers.summary: Public health organizations can benefit greatly from infectious disease epidemic forecasting to guide and support interventions and policies that reduce morbidity. papers.title: Rising Tuberculosis Presentations in Ontario, Canada Are Not Explained by Community SARS-CoV-2 Activity: A Population-Based Time-Series Study
papers.summary: BackgroundTuberculosis (TB) notifications have increased in several high-income countries since 2020. papers.summary: BackgroundZika virus local transmission has been reported in at least 97 countries and territories, but the sources, routes, and determinants of cross-country spread remain incompletely understood. papers.summary: BackgroundDosing guidance for children with leprosy remains operationally challenging. papers.summary: Seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) is an important malaria prevention strategy used widely in areas of West Africa with highly seasonal transmission. papers.title: BT-115386, a MAT2A inhibitor, targets MTAP-deficient nasopharyngeal carcinoma via c-Myc and p53 modulation
papers.summary: MTAP homozygous deletion occurs in 37.5% of Epstein-Barr virus-associated nasopharyngeal carcinomas (NPCs). Chan et al. demonstrate that the oral MAT2A inhibitor BT-115386 achieves robust tumor suppression by targeting PRMT5 to degrade c-Myc and restore p53 signaling in NPC preclinical models, establishing MAT2A/PRMT5 inhibition as a promising precision strategy for MTAP-deficient NPC.

papers.title: Gut microbiome-derived disease-associated indices for non-invasive detection of chronic diseases
papers.summary: Yin et al. develop SPECTRA, a microbiome-based framework that integrates phenotype-associated microbial representation indices to assess multiple chronic diseases from stool metagenomes. The model generalizes across independent cohorts, provides ranked and interpretable phenotype profiles, and is deployed through the xMICARE web platform.

papers.title: Expanded repeat RNAs drive aberrant cortical network activity in benign adult familial myoclonus epilepsy
papers.summary: Suga et al. establish patient-derived cortical organoids that recapitulate neuronal network hyperexcitability in benign adult familial myoclonus epilepsy (BAFME). Transcriptomic and electrophysiological analyses reveal disease-associated neuronal alterations, while antisense oligonucleotides targeting expanded repeat RNA attenuate hyperexcitability, highlighting a potential therapeutic strategy.

papers.title: XPO5 regulates ferroptosis via MITF-ACSL4 signaling to drive CRPC progression and serves as a druggable target
papers.summary: Wang et al. show that XPO5 drives CRPC progression by suppressing ferroptosis through the MITF-ACSL4 axis. They identify an XPO5-targeting molecular glue degrader that induces ferroptosis in cellular, CDX, and PDX models, supporting its translational potential.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal dynamics of adoptively transferred stem-like CD8+ T cells in the tumor microenvironment following vaccination
papers.summary: Hermans et al. show that adoptive cell therapy combining stem-like CD8+ T cells with intravenous vaccination reshapes the tumor environment to promote immune infiltration and tumor control. The findings reveal how high-quality T cells and systemic vaccination can work together to overcome barriers limiting cancer immunotherapy for advanced tumors.

papers.title: Temporal control of CAR expression by a tumor-targeting albumin adapter and logic gating enhances CAR-T cell therapy for solid tumors
papers.summary: Chen et al. develop MANAGE CAR-T cells that employ an artificial-antigen-sensing synNotch receptor to gate CAR expression and an albumin-based tumor-targeting adapter bearing the artificial antigen for priming. Adjusting the adapter dosing schedule enables tumor-restricted and intermittent CAR expression. These temporally tuned CAR-T cells exhibit reduced exhaustion and improved efficacy against solid tumors.

papers.title: Distinct T cell subsets associated with responses to different neoadjuvant treatments in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma
papers.summary: Song et al. find that neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy maintains immunoresponsive CXCL13+ CD8+ T cells, with responders showing a shift toward a less exhausted, progenitor-like phenotype, whereas chemoradiotherapy reduces this compartment and enriches PD-1- effector CD8+ T cells. Their findings provide a cellular rationale for optimizing the sequencing of immunotherapy and radiotherapy.

papers.title: FDA again turns back Capricor Duchenne cell therapy
papers.summary: In an unusual statement, the FDA accused Capricor of “serious data integrity violations” that compromised its study findings and led to deramiocel’s second rejection since 2025.

papers.title: Will the first approved psychedelic become a blockbuster?
papers.summary: Compass and Usona are vying for an FDA first, but pricing, payer coverage and patient access could determine the commercial winner.

papers.title: Erasca data add to pressure facing Revolution’s breakthrough cancer drug
papers.summary: Rasonque is already off to one of the best oncology launches in history. But certain limitations leave an opportunity that companies like Erasca — which is nearing the start of a Phase 3 trial — may be able to exploit.

papers.title: Celldex drug stumbles in eczema; Epigenetic editing startup cuts staff
papers.summary: Wall Street analysts rushed to Celldex’s defense following the setback. Elsewhere, Isomorphic Labs cut a cancer-focused deal with Merck and Teva’s research chief accepted a new job.

papers.title: This week in charts: Biotech investors’ China bets are already paying off
papers.summary: This year, companies built around medicines from China have sped toward acquisitions or IPOs. Meanwhile, Summit is no longer the Wall Street darling it was in 2024.

papers.title: Sanofi gains FDA clearance for Gaucher disease pill
papers.summary: The approval culminates a winding development journey for Infilbray, and provides Sanofi with a new source of income ahead of Dupixent’s looming patent expiration.

papers.title: China could ‘corner’ biopharma sector with new plan, US panel warns
papers.summary: A commission called on U.S. lawmakers to act quickly to prevent an “overdependence” on China that could leave American patients “vulnerable to supply chain weaponization.”

papers.title: With FDA nod, Regeneron brings an RNAi drug to autoimmune disease
papers.summary: The product of a collaboration with Alnylam, Livsayis is now Regeneron’s first marketed RNAi drug and will compete against established medicines from AstraZeneca and Argenx.

papers.title: ‘Selling and marketing snake oil’: The debate over compounded GLP-1s
papers.summary: Proponents of compounding argue it increases access, lowers prices and helps patients who may need individualized versions of a drug. But there are serious concerns, experts said at the HLTH conference.

papers.title: White House pulls nomination for FDA nominee Overton
papers.summary: The sudden end of Heidi Overton’s candidacy likely ensures a Democrat-controlled Congress will choose the FDA’s next leader — but shouldn’t disrupt the agency, analysts say.

This phase II trial evaluates whether a multi-antigen vaccine called STEMVAC improves disease-free survival after surgery in patients with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) and moderate or extensive residual cancer burden. TNBC has an aggressive clinical course and poorer disease-free survival compared to other subtypes.
